analytic.title: Generation of Schedulable Real-Time Component Implementations

div.p: In model based approaches for real-time systems (RTS) development, an iterative process that consists in the early stage verification of real-time constraints fulfillment according to a given design is usually performed in order to detect as early as possible unfeasible designs. Schedulability analysis allows this early verification of timing constraints according to so called Schedulability Analysis Model (SAM). This paper proposes a configurable framework for implementation synthesis of component oriented specification that is able to preserve the SAM timing properties that are validated at an early stage of the RTS design.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Component-oriented high-level specifications are gaining importance in the development of real-time and embedded software [1][3] [8]. Usually, components interact asynchronously via communication points called ports. Activation of a component occurs when a given data/event is received on the input port. Once activated, the component follows a run-to-completion semantics and may produce a data/event on one of its output ports at the end of its execution. This paradigm has a number of benefits such as encapsulation and decoupling of interactions. While this paradigm is gaining popularity, research provides support for the verification of non-functional requirements (NFP) of component-based models [10] [11]. A major objective is to support the verification of NFP requirements in early stages of the design process, in order to correct design errors before the implementation phase. The main difficulty of providing such a support is the possible lack of information about architectural aspects that are relevant to assess non-functional requirements against system capabilities such as computation, communication and storage resources. If this information is unavailable, hypotheses on these systems aspects have to be made. These should cover the threading strategy of the system and the allocation of software modules to system resources. The hypotheses also depend on the schedulability analysis which plays a key role for the verification of system timing constraints [9] [12].

A system configuration should be further refined in later design phases for instance with respect to the threading strategy. The properties of a validated threading strategy must be preserved in later design phases in order to keep the results of the analysis valid. Note that code generators or middleware solutions often use their own threading strategy, e.g. the CORBA Component Model (CCM) [4] uses the threading mechanism of the underlying ORB. In this paper we propose to enrich a configurable execution platform called eC3M [5] with the capability to preserve the characteristics of the evaluated threading strategy by means of a rich set of patterns for communication aspects, activation events, threads creation and management policies.

The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 introduces a small example based on the MARTE component model complemented with the artifacts required for schedulability analysis. In section 3, we introduce the model driven execution framework eC3M which is based on an extension of the UML component model. Section 4 shows how the example can be refined for the eC3M component model. Section 5 concludes the paper.

div.head: Early-stage analysis method
div.p: In order to perform schedulability analysis at early stages of the design process, a well-formed analyzable model called a Schedulabilty Analysis Model (SAM) is defined [12] [14] since an early design model may not contain all the information needed to perform schedulability analysis. The definition of a SAM model in case of component-oriented specifications has two steps. The first consists of gathering the components structure and the basic behavioral units of these components, the second of defining the workload behavior of the system, i.e. a description of end-to-end computations of interest for schedulability analysis. An end-to-end computation is a chain of operation activations representing a critical path for the 978-1-4244-6850-8/10/$26.00 ©2010 IEEE application. Each end-to-end computation is specified along with (i) the characterization of the occurrence pattern of the events activating critical path executions (e.g. periodic, sporadic, etc.) and (ii) the maximum time of a critical execution path (deadline). It is also necessary to specify the computation requirements of each end-to-end computation, which is derived from the worst-case execution time of operations belonging to end-to-end computation on the target processor. In this way the workload behavior of the system is specified.

Once the workload behaviour has been specified inside the SAM model, it is necessary to identify the so-called schedulable resources. These are units of execution taken into account by the scheduler of the system, called tasks in scheduling literature. Schedulable resources are defined by assigning the execution of the end-to-end computations to them, i.e. generating the task model. Different types of assignments exist in the literature [10][9] [16]. The results of schedulability analysis are related to the task model and changing the task model, while leaving the workload behavior unchanged, can lead to different results. Once a task model has to be found schedulable, our objective is to solve the problem of producing design refinements in later design phases which are consistent with this task model.

The following subsections introduce the abovementioned modeling concepts for SAM through a comprehensible example. Actually the example is modeled using UML-MARTE [3] diagrams in order to automatically verify the schedulability of the model using the tool chain Optimum for MAST [14][15]. Figure 1 shows an example of a component model in which three different components communicate via data flow ports. Component C 1 is connected to C 2 (data type A) and C 2 is connected to C 3 (data type B). The three components are allocated on the same ExecHost processor.

div.head: Workload behavior
div.p: Figure 2 shows two end-to-end computations of interests for schedulability analysis.

div.head: Task model
div.p: The workload behavior described in Figure 2 needs to be mapped to a task model. For sake of simplicity, we show the scenario-based mapping [16] which is also one of the most used. The idea is to regroup all the operations executed at the same rate and belonging to the same linear end-to-end computation to the same task. In our example we obtain two tasks, Task 1 and Task 2 activated by the events e 1 and e 2 , depicted in Figure 2. Deadlines for the two tasks are D 1 and D 2 respectively. Let us assume that T1=D1 and T2=D2 and let us now apply the fixed priority rate monotonic schedulability test with a rate monotonic priority assignment, i.e. the shorter the period, the higher the priority [13]. Under these assumptions the test is exact (no false negative or false positive) and reports that this task model is schedulable. In order to ensure validity of analysis at the implementation level, successive refinements should be compatible with this task model, i.e. the task model must be implemented by the execution infrastructure.Table 1

div.head: eC3M component model
div.p: eC3M is a model based driven approach that supports the transformation of a component model that is enriched with the UML profiles MARTE and FCM [5] towards an object-oriented model from which a standard code generator will produce executable code. eC3M does not presume any specific task model, but provides access to the operating system resources, typically threads with an OS supported scheduling policy (such as fixed priority). In the sequel, we sketch the refined component model and its characteristics (ports, connectors and containers) before we study the realization of the example with this model.

The component model used by eC3M is based on the flexible component model (FCM) that has been defined in the project Flex-eWare as a unification of the component model in UML [2], Fractal [1] and CCM [2]. In comparison with UML, FCM offers basically three additional concepts: (1) extended ports that are not only characterized by their type but also by their kind, (2) connections between parts of a composite are typed with connectors, and (3) containers that embed components.

Connectors are a way to specify the type and implementation of an interaction mechanism.. There are two specific data flow connector types which correspond to two different ways to consume data: either via polling or by being called whenever new data arrives (push). In case of the former, the consumer uses his own thread to retrieve data; in case of the latter a push operation is executed either by a middleware or the publisher thread.

A container is a well known design pattern (container/wrapper) enabling the encapsulation of a component. As in QoS4CCM [7], the container consists of an arbitrary number of interceptors that intercept incoming or outgoing calls, for instance for tracing -as used in the next section.

div.head: Refinement and implementation
div.p: The objective of this section is to show how the example shown in section 2 is implemented with the eC3M approach. From a user perspective, we need to model the components of Figure 1 and their assembly. Figure 3 shows the specification of the components C 1 , C 2 and C 3 of the example, Figure 4 their assembly (role of timers is discussed below). C 1 and C 2 own operations op 11 and op 21 respectively, which are the first in the chain of activations shown in Figure 2. Therefore, these two operations must be provided with an initial execution thread. In the sequel, we show how the following aspects are modeled 1. Creating initial threads 2. Simulation of external events via timers 3. Interaction between the components

div.head: Figure 4: System implementation
div.p: Creating initial threads: Initial activation in eC3M is done via ports that provide the specific interface ILifeCycle. In case of the example, we combine this mechanism with an interceptor for the activation port: the connector "UseSpecificThread". Thus, the activations operations of C1 and C2 are called during the application startup and executed in a thread with the priority obtained from analysis results.

Simulation of external events via timers: Due to the preceding step, the activations operations of C1 and C2 are called during the application startup and executed in a thread with the priority obtained from analysis results.

The implementation is based on the assembly in Figure 4: the port pt of C 1 is connected with a passive Timer, which must of course be configured with the periods T 1 =200ms and T 2 =100ms respectively. The period is a configuration property of the PassiveTimer component and a value is assigned (see section 2).

A suitable implementation of C 1 's activation in C++ is given by the code fragment below (C 2 is identical if you replace the call of op 11 with op 21 ). while (true) { op11 (); pt->nextPeriod (); // wait for n. } Component interaction: op 11 has to activate op 21 of C 2 at the end of its computation. The implementation of op 11 does it by producing a new data value and emitting it via "push" to port p21. This is the only method needed in our case, since there is no data dependency between the two tasks which would otherwise require a "pull" operation.

Tracing: a container based interception mechanism is the production of traces of all interaction. We have implemented a trace connector for OTF (open trace format [6]) which produces a trace event at the entry and exit of an operation. The trace can be visualized via the traceview plug-in of the g-eclipse (geclipse.eu) project. The timestamps provide thus complementary information to the analysis results (which are often too pessimistic).

div.head: Summary and preliminary footprint
div.p: We have shown that a simple component based example can be executed in a way that complies with the results from schedulability analysis. The use of specific threads, interaction mechanisms and tracing is specified at a high level of abstraction -we profit from the flexibility in eC3M which would for instance also enable distributed variants of the interactions. The generated model (after transformations) and code is quite small and no large middleware library is required (the binary requires the standard libraries pthread and rt as well as the OTF trace library). The containers themselves add a negligible overhead, the thread and trace interceptors that are contained are quite small resulting in a binary of about 40K.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this paper, we have shown a model based approach based on UML/MARTE which comprises schedulability analysis and the mapping towards an execution infrastructure which takes the analysis results into account, i.e. the allocation of activities to tasks of a certain priority. In addition, the execution infrastructure provides declarative mechanisms that enable a tracing of interactions. The trace completes the approach, since the trace results are complementary with analysis results.

An issue for future work is the automatic choice of interaction mechanisms depending on the task model. For instance, the allocation to different tasks is incompatible with a data push executed by the caller thread (currently, the user has to choose). This implies an integration of Optimum and eC3M with good user guidance, as well as an extension and tailoring of the container/container libraries to analysis methods.

figure.figDesc: Figure 2. Workload behavior model. The end-to-end computations E 1 and E 2 are activated by the external events e 1 and e 2 -two periodic events with periods T 1 =200ms and T 2 =100ms, respectively. The event e 1 activates the component C 1 , actually the execution of its operation op 11 . The end of the execution of op 11 activates the execution of the operation op 21 of the component C 2 while the end of the execution of op 21 triggers the operation op 12 of the component C 1 . The second end-to-end computation E 2 shows a chain of activations involving the operation op 22 of the component C 2 and the subsequent activation of the op 31 of the component C 3 . Note that E 1 has a deadline D 1 =T 1 and E 2 has a deadline D 2 =T 2 . Execution times for each operation are also shown.
